ai_stories.headline: TSMC posts a record quarter, shares still slip
facts: Q3 2026 revenue NT$1,494.24bn (US$46.72bn), +50.9% y/y; net income NT$763.06bn, +68.7% y/y
Q4 guidance US$52.3bn to 54.3bn, gross margin 65% to 67%
US-listed shares -1.8% on 15 Oct after -5.3% intraday (AP); reason (margin guidance, spending) single-source
ai_stories.paragraph: TSMC is a factory for other companies' chip designs, so it sells manufacturing, not products with its own logo. Think of a bakery that bakes every brand's cakes. Its third-quarter revenue was US$46.72bn, up 50.9% from a year earlier, and net income rose 68.7%. Gross margin, the share of each sale left after production costs, was 66.4%. Why would shares fall after a record? Markets trade on the future: reports said investors focused on softer margin guidance (65% to 67% for the next quarter) and heavy spending. That reason comes from a single source, though, and the figures still await board approval.

ai_stories.headline: A Chinese memory claim helps knock 7.6% off Korea's market
facts: CXMT president Cao Kanyu on 10 Oct: server DDR5 modules on 4F2 cells by year-end
4F2 vs 6F2: roughly 30% to 50% more density in theory
Launch is not volume production; may only partly use 4F2; Samsung 4F2 not before 2028
Kospi -7.57% to 5,554.22 on 15 Oct; Samsung -9.48%, SK hynix -11.06%; 20-minute circuit breaker
ai_stories.paragraph: A memory chip stores data in tiny cells, each holding one bit, so packing cells tighter means more memory per chip. Most DRAM today uses a cell layout called 6F², and CXMT, China's largest DRAM maker, says it plans server memory modules with a 4F² layout by year-end. Four units of area instead of six could mean roughly 30% to 50% more density, but that is theory, not measured. A launch is also not mass production, and reports say the products may only partly use 4F². Samsung's version is not expected before 2028. On 15 Oct Kospi fell 7.57%, with worries about Chinese supply, AI returns and US inflation all cited, so how much this claim mattered is unclear.

ai_stories.headline: Anthropic reportedly tells investors of $16.8bn quarterly revenue
facts: Q3 2026 revenue about USD 16.8bn, +45% q/q, per FT and attendees (not a filing, unverified)
Second straight quarter of adjusted profitability; USD 1.70 revenue per USD 1 of compute
Q2 growth over 140% on Claude Code demand
No September run rate or full-year outlook; some investors disappointed
IPO reportedly planned for November; valuation talk USD 2tn to under 1.5tn
ai_stories.paragraph: Revenue is money coming in; adjusted profit is profit after leaving out some costs, such as stock-based pay. Anthropic, which makes Claude, reportedly told investors at a private meeting that third-quarter revenue was about USD 16.8bn, up about 45% from the second quarter, with USD 1.70 of revenue for each USD 1 spent on computing power. That growth is slower than the second quarter's jump of over 140%, when Claude Code demand surged. The key caveat: none of this comes from a public filing, and it is unverified. It also gave no September annualised rate or full-year outlook, and some investors were disappointed. An IPO is reportedly planned for November, with valuation talk ranging from USD 2 trillion down to under USD 1.5 trillion.

ai_stories.headline: Nvidia's chief says CoreWeave needs no backstop
facts: Nvidia owns about 10% of CoreWeave, supplies and helped finance it
Huang in Stockholm on 15 Oct: no backstop needed, cost of capital decreasing (no figures)
5-year CDS record 1,194.5bp intraday (ICE), implying over 60% default probability
Shares -15.5% on 14 Oct, +5.9% on 15 Oct after -9.5% intraday (AP)
ai_stories.paragraph: CoreWeave is a landlord for computing power: it rents AI companies racks of Nvidia graphics chips. Nvidia owns about 10% of it, supplies its equipment and has helped finance its growth. Critics call that circular financing, meaning money flows round in a loop between supplier and customer. How worried is the market? Insurance against CoreWeave's debt defaulting hit a record 1,194.5 basis points, implying over a 60% chance of default within five years. Nvidia's Jensen Huang said CoreWeave needs no backstop and that its cost of capital is decreasing. He gave no figures, so that remains an open question. Shares fell 15.5% on 14 Oct, then closed up 5.9% on 15 Oct.

lens.mechanics: Gold competes with cash and bonds as a store of wealth. When the after-inflation return on bonds falls, or the dollar loses buying power, holding gold costs less and demand rises. When money tightens, the reverse happens.
lens.data: Three forces. First, inflation is building in the pipeline: producer prices are up 6.3% y/y, consumer prices 3.7%. Second, the real 10-year yield eased to 2.78% from 2.84%, still a high real return but a smaller headwind, which helped gold today. Third, spending holds up while hiring has stalled at +29k. The template says tightening into a slowdown later turns to easing, which favours gold. Today differs because inflation is still rising, so markets price hikes first.
lens.unsustainable: Interest takes about 21% of federal revenue (Q2 2026), like a family whose loan bill grows faster than its pay. Each hike adds to it. These are rough indicators.

longview.cycle: Debt keeps growing faster than revenue, now 6.5 times a year's revenue. The big change over the year is real rates: the real 10-year yield went from 2.3 points below real growth to 0.6 points above it, the condition under which debt burdens grow on their own. Fast nominal growth keeps the ratios steady for now. That reads as late in the cycle, in a tightening phase rather than a printing one.
longview.asset_classes: While real yields are high, cash earns a real return. Long-term bonds carry the risk that heavy debts are later eased with printing. Stocks depend on growth holding up under tighter money. Gold has tended to do best in the printing phase, not the tightening phase, so the framework treats it as a diversifier, not a timing call.
